title: How Much Do Instructional Reforms Actually Improve Schools? schools/2026/08
author: Rick Hess
summary: In this Education Week 'Rick Hess Straight Up' interview, Hess talks with Harvard's Jal Mehta and Radford University's Max Yurkofsky about their new book, A Chance to Solve Their Own Problems, a study of whether school-level 'improvement science' methods (Data Wise, Instructional Rounds, and similar continuous-improvement cycles) actually improve outcomes. Drawing on four case studies and nearly 200 interviews, Mehta and Yurkofsky conclude these methods are not self-executing: success depends on mundane, human factors, pacing, culture, politics, and measurement, more than on the sophistication of the method itself. They describe a recurring 'Spinning Wheels' pattern in which promising reforms are implemented overzealously from the top, with leaders adopting only the parts that fit their existing worldview. The conversation closes on a genuine success story, Chicago's ninth-grade on-track initiative, which raised graduation rates more than 25 percentage points over 20 years, as an example of what sustained, carefully attended-to improvement work can accomplish.
points: Mehta and Yurkofsky's new book studies whether school 'improvement science' methods (Data Wise, Instructional Rounds, and similar cycles) actually deliver results, based on four case studies and nearly 200 interviews.
Their central finding: these methods are 'not self-executing,' they require skilled, human interpretation of data and sustained relational trust, not just adoption of a framework.
They describe a recurring 'Spinning Wheels' pattern, echoing Hess's own decades-old book of that title, in which reforms are implemented overzealously and abandoned before taking root.
A key enabling condition is the right 'relational container,' a space where staff trust each other enough to share what is and isn't working without fear of repercussions.

Chicago's 9th-grade on-track initiative, which raised graduation rates more than 25 percentage points over 20 years by carefully tracking struggling freshmen, is cited as proof that sustained, well-attended improvement efforts can succeed.
quotes: Countless schools have tried to solve their own problems through continuous improvement and design methods—things like Data Wise, Instructional Rounds, and other cycles of inquiry.
The biggest lesson is that these methods are not self-executing; doing them well requires a very human process of interpreting data, developing new ideas, and building momentum for change.
There was a Spinning Wheels quality to these reforms: They were a hot thing, poorly implemented, which gave way to the next thing.
Finally, you need the right “relational container”—a space where people trust each other enough to share what’s working and what isn’t, without fear of repercussions.
Chicago raised graduation rates by more than 25 percentage points over 20 years by carefully tracking struggling 9th graders and building systems to support them.
Change is possible, but only when people carefully attend to those obstacles.
